<teammate-message teammate_id="team-lead" summary="Explore ai-research DLe datatypes">
Explore /Users/havarddaleng/Documents/git/repos/ardoq/ardoq-ai-research/ardoq-ai-research (very thorough).

Context: `ontology/src/pipeline/` generates Gremlin queries from DLe ontology fragments (`ontology/data/dl/foundation.dle`, `ontology/data/dl-inferred/group*.dle`) using the prompt `ontology/src/pipeline/prompts/gen_query.txt`. We are porting this to emit SPARQL for GraphLake (an RDF store). Already known: the pipeline structure, gen_queries.py/gen_report.py/infer_dl.py, and that `@db` annotations carry TinkerPop identifiers. Do not re-report those.

Answer with file:line evidence, "not found" if absent:

1. DATATYPES IN THE DLe: how are datatypes declared for fields in `ontology/data/dl/foundation.dle` and `metaschema.dle`? List every distinct datatype used (xsd:string, xsd:decimal, xsd:dateTime, enumerations, etc.) and quote 3-4 field declarations showing the syntax. Are numeric fields declared numeric, or as strings? This matters because the generated query must compare `"4"` vs `4`.
2. Does the DLe anywhere carry IRI information suitable for SPARQL — `@prefix`, `@ontology`, or an `@db <IRI>` form where the IRI is something other than the bare DL name? Check ALL .dle files, not just foundation.dle. Also check `ontology/doc/` (it reportedly holds OWL/Protégé files) and any .ttl/.omn/.owl files.
3. `metaschema.dle` — what is it, what does it declare, and does it define the storage-mapping annotations (`@db`, `@storage`, `@label`)? Quote the key parts. Is there anything in it that is TinkerPop-specific and would need an RDF counterpart?
4. Does `ontology/src/ardoq/air/*.clj` (the Clojure metamodel→ontology extractor) emit RDF/OWL/Turtle, and what IRI base does it use? Compare with `base-iri "http://ardoq.com/ontology/"` in ardoq_owl.clj — is there any code emitting `data.ardoq.com` IRIs?
5. Is there ANY mention anywhere in the repo (docs, TODO.md, planning/*.md, commit messages, code comments) of SPARQL, RDF, GraphLake, or a plan for the SPARQL port, beyond README.md:87? Check `ontology/src/tools/planning/*.md` and `ontology/doc/description.md` carefully.
6. `ontology/experiments/owl-code-generation/` — what does it do, and is it relevant to generating queries or to IRI mapping?

Report concisely: numbered answers, file:line refs, exact quotes where they answer the question. No narrative.
</teammate-message>

<system-reminder>
Other agents active in this session, addressable via SendMessage({to: name, message}): main, api-probe, graphlake-probe, monorepo-probe.
</system-reminder>

- gh-stack: Manage stacked branches and pull requests with the gh-stack GitHub CLI extension. Use when the user wants to create, push, rebase, sync, navigate, or view stacks of dependent PRs. Triggers on tasks involving stacked diffs, dependent pull requests, branch chains, or incremental code review workflows.
- implementation-plan: Produce a terse, fully-informed implementation plan for a specific piece of functionality — one that names exact files/layers/endpoints to touch, backed by having actually checked the code (including dependent/backend repos), with zero narrative clutter. Use when the user asks "lay out how we'd implement X", "what's the wiring needed for X", "give me an implementation plan", or similar — especially after a discussion has already established scope and the user wants the result distilled. NOT for exploratory "how does this work" mental-model requests (use mindmap for those), and NOT a substitute for actually writing the code.
- mindmap: Build a high-level, holistic conceptual map of how something in a codebase works — a whole codebase, a feature, a subsystem, a flow, or any specific thing the user points at. Use this when the user wants to *understand how something works* at an intuitive, big-picture level rather than a line-by-line walkthrough or a code edit. Triggers on requests like "explain how X works", "give me a mental model of", "how does this fit together", "map out", "I want to understand the architecture/flow of", "walk me through conceptually", "make sense of this codebase". NOT for making code changes, doing detailed code review, or answering a narrow factual lookup where a one-line answer suffices.
- tune: Extract the user's corrections and preferences from the current conversation and write them into the persistent behavioural instructions (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and the project memory directory). Use when the user says "tune", "update your instructions", "remember how I want you to work", "apply my feedback to your behaviour", or after a conversation where they corrected style, process, or output format. NOT for saving factual/project knowledge (that is ordinary memory) and NOT for one-off instructions that apply only to the current task.
- create-agent: Creates a new pydantic-ai agent for the Ardoq AI backend. Use when the user wants to add a new agent, build a new chat capability, or asks "create an agent for X".
- create-api: Creates a new API client function for calling ardoq-api endpoints. Use when adding backend integration, wrapping a Clojure endpoint, or when user asks "create an API for X".
- create-postmortem: Writes a post-mortem markdown file under docs/post-mortems/ and publishes it to Confluence (AIP space, "Post Mortems" parent). Use when the user wants to document an incident, write a post-mortem, or RCA.
- create-tool: Creates a new tool function for AI agents. Use when the user wants to add a tool, create a data fetching function, or asks "create a tool for X".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

(ns ardoq.air.ardoq-owl
  (:require [ardoq.air.ont-base :as base]
            [tawny.owl :as o]
            [clojure.string :as str]
            [taoensso.timbre :as log])
  (:import [java.io File]
           [java.util Collection]
           [org.semanticweb.owlapi.formats DLESyntaxDocumentFormat
                                           FunctionalSyntaxDocumentFormat
                                           RDFXMLDocumentFormat
                                           TurtleDocumentFormat]
           [org.semanticweb.owlapi.model OWLDataFactory IRI OWLDataRange OWLDataPropertyExpression
            OWLNamedObject OWLDocumentFormat OWLOntology]
           [org.semanticweb.owlapi.vocab OWL2Datatype OWLFacet]))

(def default-customer "ardoq")
(def default-model "metamodel")

(def ^:private base-iri "http://ardoq.com/ontology/")

(def ^:private xsd-types
  {:integer  OWL2Datatype/XSD_INTEGER
   :dateTime OWL2Datatype/XSD_DATE_TIME
   :string   OWL2Datatype/XSD_STRING
   :boolean  OWL2Datatype/XSD_BOOLEAN
   :url      OWL2Datatype/XSD_ANY_URI
   :email    OWL2Datatype/XSD_STRING})

(def ^:private rating-values #{"1" "2" "3" "4" "5"})

(defn- get-format [fmt]
  (case fmt
    :dle (DLESyntaxDocumentFormat.)
    :ofn (FunctionalSyntaxDocumentFormat.)
    :owl (RDFXMLDocumentFormat.)
    :ttl (TurtleDocumentFormat.)
    (DLESyntaxDocumentFormat.)))

;;; String utilities

(defn clean-words
  "Cleans an arbitrary string to separate out the words"
  [s sep]
  (-> s
      (str/replace #"(\p{Ll})(\p{Lu})" "$1 $2")
      str/lower-case
      (str/replace #"['\"\[\]()!@#$%^&*+=|{}]" "")
      (str/replace #"[-,:; .,]" sep)
      (str/replace "__" "_")))

(defn camel-case [s]
  (let [words (-> (clean-words s " ")
                  (str/replace "  " " ")
                  (str/split #" "))]
    (str/join "" (cons (first words) (map str/capitalize (rest words))))))

(defn pascal-case [s]
  (->> (-> (clean-words s " ")
           (str/replace "  " " ")
           (str/split #" "))

# Ardoq LLM Script

A Python script that uses PydanticAI to analyze Ardoq enterprise data CSV files via LiteLLM.

## Features

- PydanticAI agent with LiteLLM integration
- Local code execution enabled
- `get_report` tool for reading Ardoq CSV data
- Hardcoded prompt for enterprise architecture analysis

## Setup

1. Install dependencies using uv:
```bash
uv sync
```

2. Configure environment variables:
```bash
cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env with your LiteLLM credentials
```

Required environment variables:
- `LITE_LLM_API_KEY`: Your LiteLLM API key
- `LITE_LLM_ENDPOINT`: Your LiteLLM endpoint URL (e.g., https://your-endpoint.com/v1)

## Usage

Run the script:
```bash
uv run main.py
```

The script will:
1. Load the hardcoded prompt from `PROMPT` constant
2. Connect to LiteLLM using environment configuration
3. Use the `get_report` tool to read Ardoq CSV data
4. Analyze the data and provide insights

# Ardoq LLM Script

A Python script that uses PydanticAI to analyze Ardoq enterprise data CSV files via LiteLLM.

## Features

- PydanticAI agent with LiteLLM integration
- Local code execution enabled
- `get_report` tool for reading Ardoq CSV data
- Hardcoded prompt for enterprise architecture analysis

## Setup

1. Install dependencies using uv:
```bash
uv sync
```

2. Configure environment variables:
```bash
cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env with your LiteLLM credentials
```

Required environment variables:
- `LITE_LLM_API_KEY`: Your LiteLLM API key
- `LITE_LLM_ENDPOINT`: Your LiteLLM endpoint URL (e.g., https://your-endpoint.com/v1)

## Usage

Run the script:
```bash
uv run main.py
```

The script will:
1. Load the hardcoded prompt from `PROMPT` constant
2. Connect to LiteLLM using environment configuration
3. Use the `get_report` tool to read Ardoq CSV data
4. Analyze the data and provide insights

1. DATATYPES IN THE DLe
Declared with `⊤ ⊑ ∀field.<type>` (range restriction), datatype after `xsd:`. Distinct types found across `ontology/data/dl/*.dle`: `xsd:string`, `xsd:boolean`, `xsd:integer`, `xsd:decimal`, `xsd:dateTime`, `xsd:date`, plus nominal-value enumerations `{"a","b",...}` (string-literal sets), and bounded numeric ranges `xsd:integer[≥1 ⊓ ≤5]` / `xsd:decimal[≥1 ⊓ ≤5]`.

Examples (`foundation.dle`):
- `criticality`: `⊤ ⊑ ∀criticality.{"1", "2", "3", "4", "5"}` (foundation.dle:275) — ordinal 1-5 score declared as a set of STRING literals, not integers.
- `complexity`: `⊤ ⊑ ∀complexity.xsd:integer` (foundation.dle:331) — same kind of numeric concept, declared genuinely numeric.
- `maturity`: `⊤ ⊑ ∀maturity.xsd:integer[≥1 ⊓ ≤5]` (foundation.dle:393) — numeric with bounds facet.
- `marketDifferentiation`: `⊤ ⊑ ∀marketDifferentiation.xsd:decimal[≥1 ⊓ ≤5]` (foundation.dle:385).
- `contactEmail`: `⊤ ⊑ ∀contactEmail.xsd:string` (foundation.dle:347).
- `liveStartDate`/`liveEndDate`: `xsd:dateTime` (foundation.dle:355,363).
- `approved`: `xsd:boolean` (foundation.dle:243/metaschema.dle "approved" analog).
- `applicationOwnershipState`: `{"Managed","Nominated","Owned","Unowned"}` (foundation.dle:213) — string-enum, not xsd:string.

Answer to "numeric fields declared numeric or as strings": MIXED, inconsistently. Ordinal 1-5 rating fields (`criticality`, `businessStrategicFit`, `functionalFit`, `featuresAndUsability`, `technicalIntegrity`, `technicalStrategicFit`, `maintainabilityAndAgility`) are declared as string-literal enumerations `{"1",...,"5"}` (foundation.dle:251,259,267,275,425,433,441). Genuinely computed/numeric fields (`complexity`, `businessStrategicFitValue`, `functionalFitValue`, `featuresAndUsabilityValue`, `criticalityValue`, `businessValue`, `maturity`, `marketDifferentiation`) are declared `xsd:integer`/`xsd:decimal` (foundation.dle:282,292,302,312,324,331,385,393). So the generated query WILL need to know per-field whether to compare `"4"` (string) or `4` (numeric) — this isn't uniform and can't be inferred from "looks numeric."

2. IRI INFORMATION FOR SPARQL IN THE DLe
Not found in any `.dle` file. `@prefix`/`@ontology`/`@import` only appear as comment lines documenting the syntax spec (e.g. foundation.dle:11-13); the only live directive used is `@import "metaschema.dle"` (foundation.dle:29, foundation-core.dle:29, application-integration-management.dle:29) — a file import, not an IRI declaration. `@db` is always bare (`@db Application`, `@db criticality`, etc.) — never `@db <IRI>`, across all `.dle` files checked (foundation.dle, metaschema.dle, application-integration-management.dle, foundation-core/1a/2a/2ad/2bc/2d/2e.dle, dl-inferred/group1-6.dle).

BUT: `ontology/doc/foundation.ttl` and `ontology/doc/clean.ttl` (hand/tool-generated OWL exports, not DLe) DO carry real IRIs: base `http://ardoq.com/ontologies/2025/12/foundation/` (foundation.ttl:1,7). `ontology/doc/generated-files/foundation.omn` (OWL functional syntax) uses the same base. Purpose: defines Ardoq's storage-mapping primitives that all other `.dle` files import (`@import "metaschema.dle"`) — `Workspace`, `Component`, `field`, `reference`, `id`, `name`, `description`, `parent`/`ancestor`/`hasChild`/`descendant`, `rootWorkspace`, plus the reification machinery `ReferenceStatement`/`ReferenceDescription`/`describes`/`hasReference` for attaching fields to reference-instances. 111 lines, `ontology/data/dl/metaschema.dle`.
